levelDescription.value:
By the end of Year 10 students should have had the opportunity to design and produce at least 4 designed solutions focused on one or more of the 4 technologies contexts:
• Engineering principles and systems
• Food and fibre production
• Food specialisations
• Materials and technologies specialisations.
Students should have opportunities to experience creating designed solutions for products, services and environments.
Students use design and technologies knowledge and understanding, processes and production skills and design thinking to produce designed solutions for identified needs or opportunities of relevance to individuals and local, regional or global communities. They work independently and collaboratively. Problem-solving activities acknowledge the complexities of contemporary life and make connections to related specialised occupations and further study. Increasingly, study has a global perspective, with opportunities to understand the complex interdependencies involved in the development of technologies and enterprises.
Students specifically focus on preferred futures, taking into account ethics; legal issues; social values; and economic, environmental and social sustainability factors; and use strategies such as life cycle thinking. They use critical thinking, creativity, innovation and enterprise skills with increasing confidence, independence and collaboration. Students analyse data, evaluate design ideas and technologies, respond to feedback, and evaluate design processes used to inform designed solutions for preferred futures.
Using a range of technologies including a variety of graphical representation techniques to communicate, students generate and represent original ideas and production plans in 2-dimensional and 3-dimensional representations. These techniques will be specific to the technologies context and may include scale, perspective, orthogonal and production drawings with sectional and exploded views. Students produce rendered, illustrated views for marketing and use graphic visualisation software to produce dynamic views of design ideas and designed solutions.
Students identify the steps involved in planning the production of designed solutions. They develop detailed project management plans, incorporating elements such as sequenced time, cost and action plans, to manage design tasks safely. Students apply management plans, making adjustments when necessary, to successfully complete design tasks. They identify and establish safety procedures that minimise risk and manage projects with safety and efficiency in mind, maintaining safety standards and management procedures to ensure success.

description.value: In this unit, students investigate the engineering principles behind bridge design, with a focus on how forces, materials, and structural systems interact to create safe and effective structures. Students explore tension, compression, load distribution, and stability, and examine how material properties influence strength, durability, and sustainability. Through analysis of real-world bridges and hands-on design tasks, students develop an understanding of how engineers consider technical, environmental, and practical factors when designing engineered solutions. The unit builds students’ knowledge of materials and forces while developing their ability to apply the design process to solve authentic engineering problems.

In this assessment, students complete an examination that assesses their understanding of the engineering concepts underpinning bridge design. The exam includes questions on forces such as tension, compression, and load distribution, as well as the characteristics and properties of materials used in bridge construction. Students also explain the factors engineers must consider when designing bridges, including safety, sustainability, materials selection, and intended use. This assessment focuses on students’ ability to analyse engineering principles and apply theoretical knowledge to real-world design contexts.

description.value: In this collaborative design project, students work in groups to apply the full design process to create a paddle pop stick bridge in response to a given design scenario. Students analyse the problem, develop a design brief, research forces and materials, generate and prototype design ideas, and construct a bridge using appropriate tools and techniques. They test and evaluate their bridge against design criteria, refine their solution based on testing results, and present their final design and justification to an audience. This assessment emphasises teamwork, project management, safe production skills, and the ability to evaluate and communicate engineered solutions using engineering and sustainability considerations.

description.value: In this five-week intensive unit, students develop practical 3D modelling skills using SketchUp. Through a sequence of guided activities and short design challenges, they learn to create accurate geometric forms, use dimensions and scale, organise models with groups and components, apply materials, and present designs using scenes and appropriate views. The unit focuses on building confidence, precision and efficient modelling practices while demonstrating how digital models can be used to explore, communicate and refine design ideas. Rather than completing a formal assessment, students produce a collection of increasingly complex models that prepare them to use 3D visualisation and computer-aided design in future design projects.

In this unit, students explore sustainable living through the lens of resilience and self-sufficiency, examining how designed solutions can support survival and wellbeing in extreme or off-grid scenarios. Students investigate sustainability from ecological, economic, and social perspectives, considering how ethical decision-making, resource management, and long-term impacts influence design choices. Through analysis of real-world sustainable systems such as energy, water, food production, and shelter, students develop an understanding of how designers and engineers respond to challenges related to security, sustainability, and human needs. The unit emphasises thoughtful planning, innovation, and the responsible use of technologies to create sustainable living environments.

In this assessment, students design a sustainable doomsday shelter in response to a given scenario that requires living off the grid for an extended period of time. Students analyse the needs and constraints of the scenario, develop a design brief, and investigate systems and resources related to shelter, energy, water, food, and waste management. Using SketchUp, students create and refine a digital model of their shelter, justifying design decisions with reference to ecological, economic, and social sustainability considerations. Students evaluate their design against developed criteria, including sustainability and practicality, and communicate their solution using digital tools while demonstrating effective project planning and safe, appropriate use of technologies.

description.value: In this unit, students investigate the intersection of food specialisations and emerging technologies through the application of virtual reality (VR) in culinary contexts. Students explore how immersive digital environments can simulate kitchen safety, complex culinary techniques, and production workflows to improve efficiency and reduce resource waste. They examine the role of simulation in modern food industries, considering how virtual environments support skill development and ethical decision-making in high-risk or resource-intensive scenarios. Through the design process, students generate and represent original ideas for virtual cooking experiences, using graphical representation techniques and storyboards to communicate their design thinking. The unit emphasises innovation, user experience, and the strategic use of technologies to address contemporary challenges in food production and training for preferred futures.

description.value: In this design project, students investigate contemporary drivers of food trends to define a design opportunity within a professional culinary context. Students select a specific driver—such as sustainability, health and wellbeing, or cultural fusion—to guide the development of a designed solution. They apply divergent design thinking to generate and explore multiple concepts, evaluated against specific criteria: trend alignment, environmental sustainability, and aesthetic appearance. Through iterative refinement and the use of graphical representation techniques, students communicate a final dish design, justifying their decisions based on technical, environmental, and social factors. The production phase utilises virtual reality (VR) technology to simulate complex culinary workflows, allowing students to demonstrate production skills and manage safety and efficiency in a digital environment. Finally, students evaluate the success of their designed solution and the effectiveness of the virtual production process against the established design criteria.
description.aiNotes:
Task 1 – Identify the Driver (Define) 

Choose one modern driver of food trends to guide your design. 
Examples: 

Health and wellbeing (e.g. high-protein, low-sugar, plant-based) 

Environmental sustainability (e.g. local produce, minimal waste) 

Cultural fusion (e.g. mixing flavours or ingredients from different cultures) 

Convenience and lifestyle (e.g. meals for busy people, easy to prepare) 

Deliverable: 

A short paragraph explaining your chosen food trend driver 

 

Task 2 – Generate Ideas (Develop) 

Use divergent thinking to explore a wide range of ideas. 

Focus on one design criterion at a time. The 3 criteria are trend alignment, sustainability, appearance 

Create at least five different ideas for each criterion 

Use sketches, notes, or diagrams to show your thinking 

Deliverable: 

A3 page showing idea generation and exploration (sketches, annotations, mind maps) 

 

Task 3 – Combine and Refine 

Narrow down and improve your ideas. 

Combine your best elements into 2–3 refined concepts 

Justify why each concept could work for the restaurant 

Evaluate against the criteria to see which one best suits 

Deliverable: 

A3 page showing refined ideas with annotations and justifications 

 

Task 4 – Final Design (Deliver) 

Present your final dish design. 

Clearly show what the dish looks like (drawings, photos, or digital visuals) 

Explain how it reflects your chosen food trend driver 

Describe how it meets all three criteria 

Deliverable: 

A3 page showing your final concept with clear visuals and explanations 

 

Task 5 – Cook it in VR 

Create a video of you cooking a representation of the dish in VR.  

Evaluate how well your dish meets each design criterion 

Deliverable: 

Cooking video presentation

description.value: In this unit, students explore commercial design by examining how products are developed to meet user needs and succeed in competitive markets. Students investigate market analysis, target audiences, product design and manufacturing processes, and basic business principles such as value proposition, cost, and sustainability. Through analysis of existing commercial products and innovation case studies, students develop an understanding of how designers balance functionality, aesthetics, ethical considerations, and commercial viability. The unit emphasises innovation, enterprise skills, and informed decision-making in the development of market-ready designed solutions.

In this assessment, students complete an examination that assesses their understanding of key commercial design principles. The exam includes questions on how designers analyse needs and opportunities, consider ethical and sustainability factors, and apply innovation and enterprise skills when developing commercial products. Students demonstrate knowledge of materials, systems, and manufacturing considerations, as well as basic business concepts such as target audiences, market needs, and value creation. This assessment focuses on students’ ability to explain and apply foundational commercial design knowledge to authentic product design contexts.

description.value: In this unit, students develop an understanding of Australian and Aboriginal histories and cultures while building empathy as a core design skill. Students explore how culture, context, and lived experience influence design decisions, and examine the importance of ethical and respectful design when responding to Aboriginal perspectives. Through guided learning, students consider how designers can create solutions that acknowledge cultural significance, community needs, and social impact. The unit emphasises empathy, reflection, and responsible decision-making, encouraging students to design with awareness of Australia’s cultural diversity and shared histories.

In this assessment, students complete a designed solution task under exam-style time constraints to simulate working to a real-world deadline. Students are given an Australia-based design scenario and follow the final stages of the design process to generate, revise, evaluate, and refine a solution. Evaluation of the design must explicitly demonstrate empathy skills, including consideration of user perspectives, cultural context, and social impact. This assessment focuses on students’ ability to apply ethical, culturally informed, and reflective thinking to design decisions.

description.value: In this unit, students investigate how food and fibre enterprises use design and technology to respond to production challenges and changing consumer needs. Students examine a local agricultural industry and identify an opportunity to improve the production, handling, storage, transport or marketing of its products. They develop and evaluate alternative ideas before producing a model or prototype of their preferred solution. Throughout the design process, students consider the needs of producers and customers, as well as safety, ethics, sustainability, cost and commercial viability. The unit develops practical design skills while introducing students to innovation and enterprise within Australia’s agricultural industries.

In this unit, students investigate authentic challenges within local food and fibre industries, ranging from cattle and poultry management to horticulture and rural mechanisation. Students apply design thinking to develop solutions that improve the production, handling, storage, or marketing of agricultural goods. By focusing on the needs of a specific producer or customer, students explore safety, ethics, and commercial viability while refining their technical production skills. Through the development of a model or prototype and a corresponding commercial proposal, students engage with innovation and enterprise, balancing practical constraints with creative, sustainable design. This unit emphasises the real-world application of design technologies in an agricultural context, preparing students to critically evaluate the lifecycle and impact of their designed solutions.
description.aiNotes:
Students investigate a real problem facing a local agricultural producer and design a solution that improves how food or fibre is produced, handled, stored, transported or marketed.

This would suit country boys because it could involve cattle, fishing, cropping, poultry, horticulture, beekeeping, rural machinery or livestock rather than feeling like another classroom sustainability project.

Possible student projects

Students could design:

a safer livestock-feeding system
a portable animal shelter or shade structure
a better system for transporting produce
an egg-collection or chicken-feeding system
a water-saving trough or irrigation system
a farm-gate produce stall
protective packaging for local produce
a storage system that reduces food spoilage
a device for safely handling livestock
a modular beehive transport or storage solution
a service for connecting local producers with customers
a redesigned product made from wool, timber or another local fibre

They would not all need to make the same product. They could select an agricultural sector, identify a producer or user, and develop a solution suited to that context.

Strong assessment concept
Design brief

Design a product, service or environment that improves an aspect of a food or fibre enterprise. The solution must respond to the needs of a specific producer or customer and consider safety, ethics, sustainability, production costs and commercial viability.

Students would:

Select a food or fibre enterprise.
Investigate how the enterprise currently operates.
Identify a genuine production, handling or marketing problem.
Develop criteria with the producer or user in mind.
Generate and test alternative ideas.
Produce a model, prototype or working product.
Develop a simple commercial proposal.
Evaluate whether the solution is practical and viable.

The commercial proposal could include estimated production cost, sale price, target market, branding and how the design creates value. That brings in the innovation and enterprise emphasis of AC9TDE10K02 without turning the unit into a business subject.

description.value:
In this 8-week unit, students explore interior design through a human-centred design approach within the built environments context. They investigate how people experience and interact with interior spaces, considering client needs, ergonomics, accessibility, spatial planning, movement and aesthetic principles. Students analyse existing interiors to identify how layout, scale, proportion, lighting, colour, furniture and visual style can influence the function, comfort and experience of a space. Virtual reality (VR) is used as an immersive design tool, allowing students to experience spaces at 1:1 scale and evaluate how effectively design decisions respond to the needs of users.

Applying an iterative design process, students develop an interior environment in response to a simulated client brief. They explore the client's needs and preferences, establish design criteria, generate alternative spatial concepts and progressively refine their preferred solution. Using 3D modelling and visualisation software, students create and test their interior design through virtual walkthroughs, using feedback and observations to improve spatial layout, usability and aesthetic qualities. The unit culminates in a digital presentation and 1:1 scale VR walkthrough in which students communicate their design process, justify key interior design decisions and evaluate how effectively their solution responds to the client and identified success criteria.

Task Type: Design Project (Folio + VR Prototype + Client Presentation)

Scenario: Students are commissioned to redesign a specific, constrained interior space for a distinct client persona. The design must respond to the client’s functional needs, preferences, accessibility requirements and intended use of the space.

Part 1: The Design Folio (Investigating & Generating)

Client and Space Analysis: Students interpret the client brief and investigate the needs, preferences and behaviours of the user, alongside the functional and spatial constraints of the room.

Ideation: Students develop mood boards, annotated sketches, 2D floor plans and alternative layout concepts that explore spatial organisation, furniture placement, lighting, colour and overall visual style.

Design Development: Students establish success criteria and refine a preferred concept using feedback, ergonomic considerations and human-centred design principles.

Part 2: The Immersive Prototype (Producing)

Virtual Prototype: Using Home Design 3D VR/VisualizeR on the Meta Quest 3S, students construct a 1:1 scale virtual prototype of their interior design.

Iterative Testing: Students experience and test their design in VR, evaluating movement, scale, accessibility, furniture placement and the overall experience of the space. They document at least two significant refinements made as a result of testing and feedback.

Part 3: The Client Walkthrough (Evaluating)

Client Presentation: Students deliver a live or recorded walkthrough of their completed virtual interior.

Justification and Evaluation: Students explain and justify key design decisions and evaluate their final solution against the identified success criteria. They demonstrate how the final design responds to the client’s needs and explain how testing and refinement improved the functionality, usability and overall experience of the space.

conditions.value:
• Folio: 4–6 A3 pages (or digital equivalent) of annotated design thinking, including mood boards, scaled 2D spatial layouts, material lifecycle analyses, and iterative VR testing documentation.
• Prototype: Functional, fully rendered 1:1 scale virtual interior environment developed using specialised 3D modelling and VR software.
• Pitch: 3–5 minute multimodal recorded or live walkthrough defending spatial, aesthetic, and material choices against the design criteria.
• Duration and supervision: Completed over 5–6 weeks of integrated class time under teacher direction and monitoring, with independent development as required.

moderation.value:
Internal moderation is conducted systematically across the faculty to ensure consistency of teacher judgement against the Australian Curriculum Year 9–10 Design and Technologies achievement standards. This process includes:

*   **Standardisation (Pre-assessment):** Prior to task delivery, teachers collaboratively review the task brief, Guide to Making Judgements (GTMJ), and sample VR design folios. Benchmarks are established to ensure a common understanding of evidence required for spatial flow analysis, material lifecycle evaluations, and iterative prototyping across performance levels (A–E).
*   **Monitoring (Week 6):** Intermediate benchmarking of draft design folios (needs analysis, mood boards, and 2D floor plans) and initial 3D spatial models. Faculty members calibrate feedback to confirm that student evidence accurately documents VR testing and iterative design decisions.
*   **Moderation Conferencing (Week 9–10):** Teachers collaboratively review recorded VR walkthroughs, pitches, and completed design folios at key grade boundaries (A/B, B/C, C/D). Judgements regarding the justification of interior design choices and technical execution are calibrated against the achievement standard.
*   **Cross-Marking:** Blind cross-marking of a representative cohort sample (high, medium, low, and borderline responses) is conducted to ensure objectivity, equity, and consistency in grading standards across all classes. Selected exemplar work is archived to support future benchmarking.
